claims.text: The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA was produced by additive manufacturing.
The as-fabricated alloy has a homogeneous distribution of dual nanoprecipitates.
Oxidation at 800–1000 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressure is representative of relevant high-temperature service environments.
Nanoprecipitates act as reservoirs of reactive elements in this HEA matrix.
High-temperature exposure induces oxidation at the alloy surface.
Al and Cr diffuse from nanoprecipitates toward the oxidizing surface.
Al and Cr arriving at the surface form protective oxide layers.
In situ high-temperature TEM can capture dynamic nanoprecipitate morphology changes and interactions with a growing oxide scale.
APT can provide atom-by-atom compositional maps confirming oxidation-induced elemental redistribution.
Oxidation will produce significant microstructural evolution of the nanoprecipitates observable by in situ TEM.
APT will detect enrichment of Al and Cr at the oxide–alloy interface after oxidation.
Nanoprecipitate elemental redistribution is a key mechanism governing whether protective or non-protective oxide scales form.
Cast and wrought counterparts of this alloy have lower strength than the additively manufactured material.
Cast and wrought processing routes provide limited insight into oxidation-induced elemental redistribution.
The redistribution behavior may vary with oxidation temperature, oxygen partial pressure, and duration.
Substantially different nanoprecipitate distributions may alter the observable redistribution dynamics.
Combining in situ high-temperature TEM and APT is expected to provide mechanistic insight into oxidation-induced elemental redistribution.
The magnitude of elemental migration and its direct effect on oxidation resistance are uncertain and may depend on experimental conditions.
